1.text:
From Dark Cloud to Shining Star

In Deck 15 you learned to read starlight. Now we start the life story of the stars themselves, beginning at the very beginning. Every star you see tonight, including our Sun, started out as part of a cold, dark cloud drifting between the stars.

This deck asks one big question: how does a cold, dark cloud become a shining star? The short answer is gravity. Gravity pulls clouds of gas together into stars. The long answer involves spinning disks, blasting jets, failed stars, and the birth of planets. Deck 17 will finish the story with how stars live and die.

2.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist for this deck. Write these down as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can describe the gas and dust between the stars. I can explain why stars form in cold, dense molecular clouds. I can use infrared images from Webb and Hubble to see inside star nurseries. I can explain how gravity beats gas pressure, using the Jeans mass. I can explain why a collapsing cloud makes a disk and jets.

I can trace a protostar to the main sequence on the H-R diagram. I can explain hydrogen ignition and the 0.08-Sun lower limit. I can describe star clusters as families born together. I can explain why small stars far outnumber big ones. And I can link disks like HL Tau to how our own solar system formed. These connect to Indiana standards ES.1.3, ES.1.1, ES.2.1, ES.1.4 and ES.1.5, plus some enrichment.

3.text:
The Stuff Between the Stars

Space between the stars isn't totally empty. It holds the interstellar medium, a thin spread of gas and dust. It's so thin that it's emptier than the best vacuum we can make on Earth, but across huge distances it adds up.

About 99% of it is gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, the same ingredients that make up stars. You'll see single atoms like H and He, plus pairs like H2. The other 1% is dust.

Zoom in on one dust grain and you'll find a rocky (silicate) or graphite core, wrapped in an ice mantle made of water, methane and ammonia. These tiny grains matter a lot, because they're the seeds of future planets.

Did you know? Dust between the stars makes starlight look dimmer and redder, the same reason sunsets look red.

4.text:
Cold, Dark Nurseries

Stars are born inside molecular clouds, and these places are cold. Inside, the temperature is about 10 K, only 10 degrees above absolute zero. That's far colder than anywhere on Earth. It's so cold that hydrogen atoms pair up into H2 molecules, which is how the clouds got their name.

That creates a problem for astronomers, because H2 is nearly invisible. So they look for carbon monoxide (CO) gas instead, which glows in radio light and shows where the clouds are.

These clouds are huge. A single cloud can hold 1,000 to 3 million Suns' worth of gas, with filaments up to 1,000 light-years long. Inside are clumps of 50 to 500 Suns, and inside the clumps are smaller, denser cores. Each core is a star embryo.

Did you know? The thick dust that makes these clouds dark also shields them from starlight, which helps keep them so cold.

5.text:
Same Pillars, Two Kinds of Light

These towers are the famous Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula (M16), about 6,500 light-years away. They're columns of cool gas and dust where new stars are forming.

Compare the two pictures. Hubble photographed them in 1995 in visible light. The dust hides most of the stars, so the pillars look dark and solid. Webb photographed them again in 2022 in infrared, which sees through much of the dust to reveal new stars inside and around the pillars. Webb's view is about 8 light-years across.

Same pillars, two kinds of light, two very different pictures. This is why astronomers use telescopes that see different kinds of light, as you learned in Deck 15.

Did you know? Each pillar is several light-years tall, so our whole solar system would be a tiny speck inside one.

6.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Look closely at the two images again. Why does Webb show more newborn stars in the Pillars than Hubble did?

Is it A) infrared light passes through the dust, B) Webb is closer to the Pillars, C) the stars formed after 1995, or D) the pillars are made of hot gas? Think about Slides 4 and 5, then choose and explain your answer.

7.text:
Gravity vs Pressure

A star's whole life is a tug-of-war between two forces. Gravity pulls in. Gas pressure pushes out. For a star to form, gravity has to win.

The Jeans mass is the smallest clump that its own gravity can pull together. If a clump has more than the Jeans mass, it collapses. Two things help gravity win. Colder gas pushes less, so it collapses more easily. Denser gas pulls harder, so it also collapses more easily. That's why cold, dense cores are where stars are born.

Gravity has other opponents too. Turbulence, the swirling motion of the gas, and magnetic fields push back against collapse.

Did you know? The Jeans mass is named for James Jeans, who worked out the rule in 1902.

8.text:
A Huge Squeeze

To become a star, a cloud core has to get squeezed until it's about 1020 times denser. That's 100 billion billion times. Imagine squeezing a whole football stadium of air down into a sugar cube, and you're still not close.

Gravity does all the work. The first collapse is surprisingly fast for space: only thousands of years. The dense core falls in on itself and becomes a protostar.

As the gas falls inward, it heats up. That's because energy from falling turns into heat, the same way a meteor heats up as it falls through the air.

Did you know? Because that first collapse is so quick and hidden by dust, astronomers rarely catch one in the act.

9.text:
Spin Up, Flatten Out

Every clump has a little bit of spin. As it shrinks, something important happens: conservation of angular momentum. A shrinking, spinning cloud must spin faster. Think of a figure skater pulling her arms in and suddenly whirling much faster.

The cloud starts as a big, slow spin about 5,000 AU across. As it gets smaller, it spins faster. Gas falls in easily at the poles, where the spin is slow. But at the equator, the fast spin holds material back, so it piles up into a flat disk about 100 AU across.

That's why so many stars have disks around them, and disks are where planets are born. You saw the same idea in Deck 4, when you learned how our solar system formed.

Did you know? A disk 100 AU across is a bit bigger than Pluto's orbit around the Sun.

10.text:
Jets from Baby Stars

Baby stars are messy. As a young star starts blowing out a wind, the dusty disk blocks it at the equator. So the wind escapes the only way it can: out of the poles, as two narrow jets shooting in opposite directions. Meanwhile, the dusty disk hides the star itself.

When a jet slams into gas nearby, it makes the gas glow. That glowing knot is called a Herbig-Haro object, or HH object.

The numbers are wild. HH 30 is about 450 light-years away, and its jets travel up to 580,000 km/h. The jets of HH 1 and HH 2 stretch more than 1 light-year tip to tip.

Did you know? At 580,000 km/h, a jet could cross the distance from Earth to the Moon in less than an hour.

11.text:
Draw It: Gravity Builds a Star

Your turn to tell the story. This task matches standard ES.1.3. Draw five boxes: 1, cloud. 2, clump and core. 3, protostar and disk. 4, jets clear out. 5, a star is born.

In every box, draw gravity arrows pointing in and pressure arrows pointing out. Make the arrow sizes show who's winning. Write the temperature: about 10 K at the start and about 10 million K at the end.

Under each arrow between boxes, add a time, like thousands of years or millions of years. Finish each box with one sentence: what does gravity do at this step?

12.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Time to think like a star-maker. Which change makes a cloud core MORE likely to collapse into a star?

Is it A) cooling it down, B) heating it up, C) spreading it out thinner, or D) stirring it with more turbulence? Look back at Slide 7 and pick one. Be ready to explain why each of the others makes collapse harder.

13.text:
Protostar to T Tauri Star

A protostar is a shrinking ball of gas, heated by gravity, before fusion starts. It's like a star still under construction.

Follow the steps on the slide. In stage a, a dense core forms in the cloud. In stage b, a protostar with a disk appears while gas keeps falling in. At this point it's still wrapped in dust, so it's seen only in infrared. In stage c, a wind breaks out at the poles. In stage d, the wind has cleared away the dust, and we see a T Tauri star, visible with its disk.

T Tauri stars are young stars about the mass of the Sun or smaller that haven't started fusion yet. They're still shrinking, on their way to becoming full stars.

Did you know? T Tauri stars are named after the first one studied, a star called T Tauri in the constellation Taurus.

14.text:
Shining on Squeeze Power

Before fusion starts, how does a young star shine? By squeezing. As it shrinks, it heats and glows.

How long could squeezing alone power the Sun? About 30 million years, at the Sun's power of 3.828 × 1026 W. That sounds like a lot, but Earth is 4.54 billion years old, so gravity alone falls short. The Sun must have another power source today, and that's fusion.

But for a young star, squeeze power is exactly what it uses. A young Sun-like star shines this way for tens of millions of years before fusion kicks in.

15.text:
Tracks on the H-R Diagram

Remember the H-R diagram from Deck 15? Brighter is up and hotter is to the left. An evolutionary track is the path a star's dot traces on the H-R diagram as the star changes. The dot moves because the star's temperature and brightness change, not because the star moves through space.

The slide shows tracks for stars of 15 Suns, 3 Suns, 1 Sun and 0.5 Suns. First, the track makes a fast drop as the protostar shrinks and gets dimmer. Then it makes a slow move left as the surface heats, until it reaches the main sequence.

Timing depends on mass. Big stars race through this stage in thousands to 1 million years. Small stars take tens of millions of years.

16.text:
Fusion Switches On

When the core reaches about 10 to 12 million K, hydrogen fusion starts. Just like in Deck 14, 4 H make 1 He, and a bit of mass becomes energy.

Now the forces are balanced: gravity in, pressure out. Contraction stops, because fusion now pays the energy bill. The star has landed on the zero-age main sequence, the line on the H-R diagram where newborn stars land when hydrogen fusion starts.

Mass picks the spot. Big stars land hot and bright at the upper left. Small stars land cool and dim at the lower right. The Sun has been here about 4.5 billion years.

Did you know? Today the Sun's core is even hotter, about 15 million K, because it has slowly heated up over billions of years.

17.text:
Too Small, Too Big

Stars come in a range of sizes, but there are limits. The lower limit is 0.08 Suns, about 80 Jupiter masses. Below this, the core never gets hot enough to fuse hydrogen, and the object becomes a brown dwarf, a kind of "failed star."

Look at the mass line. Objects smaller than about 0.012 Suns, or 13 Jupiters, are planets. Between 0.012 and 0.08 Suns are brown dwarfs. Above 0.08 Suns are stars, including the Sun at 1.

Is there a top limit? Above about 150 Suns, the starlight is so strong it blows the gas away before more can fall in. But nature likes to break rules. A star called R136a1 is estimated at about 200 Suns (a 2022 estimate, down from earlier estimates of over 300). That's why the slide asks: too big?

Did you know? Brown dwarfs glow mostly in infrared and slowly cool off for the rest of time.

18.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Now a mass puzzle. A collapsing core ends up with 0.05 Suns of mass. What does it become?

Is it A) a brown dwarf, B) a red main-sequence star, C) a white dwarf, or D) a T Tauri star that later fuses H? Check the mass line on Slide 17 and make your choice.

19.text:
Stars Are Born in Families

Stars are rarely born alone. A star cluster is a family of stars born together from one cloud. One of the most famous nurseries is the Orion Nebula, about 1,300 light-years away.

The Orion Nebula holds about 2,200 young stars packed into about a dozen light-years. At its heart is the Trapezium: 4 hot, bright stars whose light makes the whole nebula glow.

Making stars is not very efficient. Only about 1% of the gas has become stars. And most young clusters don't stay together. They drift apart over time, like siblings moving away from home.

Did you know? You can see the Orion Nebula without a telescope. It's the fuzzy "star" in the middle of Orion's sword.

20.text:
Many Small Stars, Few Big Ones

The initial mass function is how many stars are born at each mass. When a cloud breaks apart, it makes many small clumps and only a few big ones.

Look at our neighbors within 21 light-years. There are 0 O stars and 0 B stars. There are 2 A stars, 1 F star, 7 G stars, 17 K stars, and a whopping 94 M stars. Big, hot stars are on one end, and small, cool stars are on the other.

Red dwarfs (M stars) are about 3 of every 4 stars nearby. That means the Sun, which feels like an ordinary star, actually outweighs most stars.

21.text:
Where Planets Are Born

A protoplanetary disk is the leftover disk around a young star, where planets form. And we have pictures of one!

This is HL Tau, about 450 light-years away. It's no more than 1 million years old. The ALMA telescope array photographed its disk in 1.3 mm radio light. Look at the dark gaps between the bright rings. Each gap might be a young planet sweeping up material as it orbits.

Our solar system went through the same story 4.57 billion years ago. Looking at HL Tau is like looking at a baby picture of our own neighborhood.

Did you know? Disks don't last long. Most young stars lose their planet-forming disks within a few million years.

22.text:
Flowchart: Cloud to Solar System

Time to put the whole story together. This task matches standard ES.2.1. Draw and label seven boxes.

1, the cloud collapses. 2, a star forms with a spinning disk. 3, dust grains stick together. 4, they grow into planetesimals. 5, planetesimals grow into protoplanets. 6, terrestrial or Jovian? Mark the frost line in this box. 7, moons, asteroids and comets form from what's left.

Add a timeline: the star is about 1 million years old early on, and the disk is gone by about 6 million years.

23.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

A new cluster forms 1,000 stars. Which kind will it have the MOST of?

Is it A) small, cool M stars, B) Sun-like G stars, C) huge, hot O stars, or D) equal numbers of each? Look back at the bar chart on Slide 20 and choose.

24.text:
Exit Ticket

You've watched a star go from cold cloud to shining sun. Show what you learned with three questions.

First, list the steps from a cold molecular cloud to a main-sequence star. Second, why does a collapsing cloud make a disk and two jets? Third, why can a star not have 0.01 Suns or 1,000 Suns of mass?

When you finish, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

25.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.3: make a diagram, flowchart or explanation of how energy cooled into protons and early elements, and how those elements formed huge stars and galaxies. Explain how gravity pulls clouds of these elements together into stars and galaxies. ES.1.4: compare the life cycles of low, medium (like our Sun) and high mass stars on the H-R Diagram, including which elements they make and whether they become red giants or go supernova.

ES.2.1: build a flowchart of the nebular theory, showing how stars, planetesimals, protoplanets, Jovian and terrestrial planets, moons and small bodies formed. ES.1.5 is introduced here: show how stars, planetary systems, star clusters, galaxies and galaxy groups fit inside each other. And ES.1.1 is review: we study space by observing every kind of light with different telescopes.
